method: Each overview was drafted by research agents from web searches. An independent fact-check then gave every claim a verdict (confirmed, corrected or unsupported) and recorded the sources it used. The fact-checkers could not open the primary pages themselves (those hosts did not answer), so the checks rest on search-engine result summaries that quote the named pages, plus a few distances computed from the catalogue coordinates; treat them as medium to low confidence. Unsupported claims, including some that the SR1, CR1, SV1 and MP1 checker could not search before its search budget ran out, were left out of the text, and corrected claims use the corrected wording. An editorial pass on 2026-10-25 then removed only clauses that state a number the app computes itself (Rule C: distance from the south pole), kept the rest of each sentence and added no claim; every change is logged in the site's edits list as was, now and why.

sites.headline: Candidate region beside Haworth, one of the pole's coldest craters
sites.overview: Haworth is one of NASA's candidate landing regions near the lunar south pole. NASA named it among 13 regions for Artemis III in August 2022 and kept it on the shorter list of nine in October 2024; in February 2026 NASA moved the first crewed landing to Artemis IV. Each region is about 15 by 15 km. This one lies beside Haworth crater, a very old crater whose shadowed floor holds some of the coldest ground measured at the pole, in places never above about 40 K. Orbiter neutron data point to hydrogen, likely water ice, in that shadowed ground.

verdicts.claim: Haworth was one of the 13 Artemis III candidate landing regions NASA named on 19 August 2022.
verdicts.finalClaim: Haworth was one of the 13 Artemis III candidate landing regions NASA named on 19 August 2022.

verdicts.claim: Haworth stayed on NASA's October 2024 list of nine candidate regions, in no priority order.
verdicts.finalClaim: Haworth stayed on NASA's October 2024 list of nine candidate regions (Peak near Cabeus B, Haworth, Malapert Massif, Mons Mouton Plateau, Mons Mouton, Nobile Rim 1, Nobile Rim 2, de Gerlache Rim 2, Slater Plain), listed in no priority order.

verdicts.claim: Each region is about 15 by 15 km within 6 degrees of latitude of the pole; a landing site is about 100 m in radius.
verdicts.finalClaim: NASA describes each candidate region as about 15 by 15 km, within six degrees of latitude of the south pole; a landing site is a spot about 100 m in radius inside a region.

verdicts.claim: The crater Haworth is named for Walter Haworth, British chemist and 1937 Nobel laureate; name approved October 2008.
verdicts.finalClaim: The crater Haworth is named for Walter Haworth, British chemist and 1937 Nobel laureate in chemistry; the name was approved in October 2008 (secondary sources only; Gazetteer unreachable).

verdicts.claim: Sources disagree on the crater's centre and size.
verdicts.finalClaim: Secondary sources disagree on the crater's size (Wikipedia 51.4 km, the-moon.us 35 km); Wikipedia puts its centre near 86.9 S, 4 W. The Gazetteer could not be opened. Coordinate check: the catalog point (-86.75, -23.67) is about 33-35 km from the crater centre (Wikipedia or repo Gazetteer value), so the region lies beside the crater, outside its rim, not on its floor.
verdicts.source: [search summary] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haworth_(crater) ; https://the-moon.us/wiki/Haworth ; distance computed from catalog coordinates

verdicts.claim: Much of the crater is permanently shadowed; parts never warm above about 40 K.
verdicts.finalClaim: A 2013 Diviner temperature study found some of the coldest maximum temperatures at the south pole inside Haworth crater, apparently never above about 40 K; the crater holds a permanently shadowed region.

verdicts.claim: A 2015 LOLA-based study (Tye et al.) dates Haworth crater to the Pre-Nectarian period.
verdicts.finalClaim: A 2015 LOLA crater-count study (Tye et al., Icarus 255) gives Haworth, Shoemaker and Faustini pre-Nectarian formation ages.

verdicts.claim: A 2023 LRO neutron study found PSRs in Haworth, Shoemaker and Faustini hold the most detectable hydrogen.
verdicts.finalClaim: A LRO neutron study (McClanahan et al., arXiv 2023, Planetary Science Journal 2024) finds hydrogen, likely water ice, in most south-pole permanently shadowed regions; within the Haworth, Shoemaker and Faustini shadowed regions the highest hydrogen sits where the ground is coldest, near the base of pole-facing slopes.

verdicts.claim: A 2026 Nature Astronomy study by a CU Boulder and Weizmann team (Aharonson lead) found cold traps gathering ice for 1.5 Gyr and singled out Haworth.
verdicts.finalClaim: Press coverage (April 2026) of a study led by Oded Aharonson (Weizmann Institute) with US collaborators, using LRO data and thermal models, says polar ice has built up for at least 1.5 billion years and that Haworth looks a more promising ice target than Shackleton. CU Boulder and the journal were not confirmed.

verdicts.claim: NASA's stated reason: land near PSRs so crews can sample undisturbed ground and learn the depth, distribution and make-up of water ice.
verdicts.finalClaim: NASA chose regions that give access to permanently shadowed areas so crews can sample undisturbed ground and learn about the depth, distribution and composition of water ice.

verdicts.claim: (from unknowns) NASA changed Artemis III in Feb 2026 and moved the first crewed landing to Artemis IV.
verdicts.finalClaim: In February 2026 NASA made Artemis III a crewed test flight in Earth orbit and moved the first crewed landing near the south pole to Artemis IV, so 'Artemis III candidate region' is a dated label.

sites.headline: High, flat patch atop Mons Malapert, a remnant basin-rim mountain
sites.overview: This region sits near the top of a large mountain on the Earth-facing side of the south pole. Informally called Malapert Massif, the mountain got the IAU name Mons Malapert in 2024 and is about 67 km across. Scientists think it is a remnant of the rim of the South Pole-Aitken basin. The candidate area is a fairly flat patch near 86 S, 0 E; the peak rises more than 5,000 m above its base, and a 3,500 m cliff is in view. NASA listed the region for Artemis III in 2022 and kept it in 2024. NASA notes good sunlight and a clear view of Earth on its rim.

verdicts.claim: IAU approved Mons Malapert (26 Aug 2024); about 67 km, centre -85.98, -1.67 E; named for crater Malapert, honouring Charles Malapert (1581-1630).
verdicts.finalClaim: The IAU Gazetteer lists Mons Malapert, adopted with approval date 26 August 2024, about 67 km across, centred near -85.98, -1.67 E, named for the nearby crater Malapert; that crater honours Charles Malapert (1581-1630), astronomer from Mons in present-day Belgium. Coordinate check: the catalog point is about 3 km from that centre, on the mountain.

verdicts.claim: Before that, 'Malapert Peak' and 'Malapert Massif' were informal names in use for decades.
verdicts.finalClaim: Before 2024 the mountain had only informal names, such as Malapert Mountain and Malapert Massif (LROC calls 'Malapert massif' an informal name). 'For decades' is not confirmed.

verdicts.claim: Malapert Massif was on the August 2022 list of 13 and the October 2024 list of nine.
verdicts.finalClaim: Malapert Massif was on NASA's August 2022 list of 13 Artemis III candidate regions and on the October 2024 list of nine.

verdicts.claim: LROC: probable remnant of the SPA basin rim, rising >5,000 m above its base; candidate site a flat area near 86 S, 0 E.
verdicts.finalClaim: LROC (Mark Robinson, 14 March 2023) describes the massif as a probable remnant of the South Pole-Aitken basin rim (formed more than 4 billion years ago) that rises more than 5,000 m above its base; the Artemis candidate area is a relatively flat area near 86 S, 0 E.

verdicts.claim: A peer-reviewed study interprets Mons Malapert and Mons Mouton as remnant SPA-rim massifs covered by hundreds of metres of later ejecta.
verdicts.finalClaim: A peer-reviewed geologic study (Wueller et al.) interprets Mons Malapert and Mons Mouton as remnant massifs of the South Pole-Aitken basin rim, buried under several hundred metres of later ejecta.

verdicts.claim: The flat area sits above a ~5,000 m cliff, with a 3,500 m cliff in view; 'might be too exciting'.
verdicts.finalClaim: The 5,000 m figure is the peak's height above its base, not a single cliff; LROC says a 3,500 m cliff is visible in the distance and its PI asked whether landing there 'might be too exciting'.

verdicts.claim: NASA: LOLA data show the Malapert Massif rim with high illumination and exceptional Earth visibility; suggested exploration site.
verdicts.finalClaim: NASA notes that LOLA data show the rim of Malapert Massif with high illumination and exceptional Earth visibility, and that the region has been suggested for future exploration.

verdicts.claim: IM-1 Odysseus (22 Feb 2024) landed near Malapert A at 80.13 S, 1.44 E, ~300 km from the pole; no mission has landed in this region.
verdicts.finalClaim: IM-1 Odysseus landed on 22 February 2024 near crater Malapert A at 80.13 S, 1.44 E (NASA), about 300 km from the pole and about 180 km from this region's centre (computed). That is a separate site. 'No mission has landed in this region' is not confirmed by a source.

verdicts.finalClaim: In February 2026 NASA made Artemis III a crewed test flight in Earth orbit and moved the first crewed landing near the south pole to Artemis IV, so 'Artemis III candidate region' is a dated label.

sites.headline: Broad, rocky top of Mons Mouton, where IM-2 Athena landed
sites.overview: Mons Mouton Plateau is NASA's informal name for the broad top of Mons Mouton, a flat-topped mountain almost 100 km across that rises about 6,000 m above the land around it. NASA added the region to its Artemis III candidate list in October 2024; it was not on the 2022 list. Flat-topped does not mean smooth: NASA says the summit is peppered with rocks, pebbles and many craters. Intuitive Machines' IM-2 Athena landed near the centre of the mountain on 6 March 2025, but came down hard and ended on its side in a small crater, which cut the mission short.

verdicts.claim: Mons Mouton Plateau is one of nine regions announced Oct 2024; not on the 2022 list of 13.
verdicts.finalClaim: Mons Mouton Plateau is one of the nine Artemis III candidate regions NASA announced in October 2024; it was not on the 2022 list of 13.

verdicts.finalClaim: LROC's Mons Mouton Plateau low-Sun NAC mosaics (P843S0306 series) cover about -85.76 to -82.85 latitude and 15.49 to 46.61 E. Coordinate check: the catalog point (-84.3, 30.6) is about 15 km from IM-2's target, inside these bounds.

verdicts.claim: Mons Mouton is about the size of Delaware, nearly 100 km across, ~6,000 m high; may be billions of years older than surroundings.
verdicts.finalClaim: Mons Mouton is a wide, relatively flat-topped mountain about the size of Delaware, almost 100 km across, rising roughly 6,000 m above the surrounding terrain; NASA says it is possibly billions of years older than its surroundings (a hedge, not settled).

verdicts.claim: NASA: hilltop peppered with small rocks, pebbles and many craters.
verdicts.finalClaim: NASA says the rolling hilltop is peppered with smaller rocks and pebbles and many craters, often in shifting shadow.

verdicts.claim: IM-2 Athena landed 6 March 2025; target -84.78, 29.13 E, 160 km from pole; ~250 m from target; on its side in a ~20 m crater; >400 MB returned.
verdicts.finalClaim: IM-2 Athena landed on 6 March 2025 near the centre of Mons Mouton. LROC gives the target as -84.78, 29.13 E, 160 km from the pole, in the central part of an Artemis candidate region. It came down harder than planned and ended on its side in a crater about 20 m wide, yet returned over 400 MB. Distance from target: NASA says more than 400 m (Intuitive Machines said 250 m).

verdicts.claim: IM-2 carried PRIME-1 drill and mass spectrometer; first chosen Shackleton connecting ridge (July 2024).
verdicts.finalClaim: IM-2 carried NASA's PRIME-1 drill payload to look for water ice. It was first to land on a ridge near Shackleton crater, then before launch was retargeted to VIPER's original destination, Mons Mouton. The July 2024 date and the mass spectrometer were not confirmed.

sites.headline: Pole-facing side of Mons Mouton, once called Leibnitz Beta Plateau
sites.overview: This region covers the southern, pole-facing part of Mons Mouton, a flat-topped mountain almost 100 km across that stands about 6,000 m above its surroundings, beside the western rim of Nobile crater. NASA's 2022 Artemis III list called it Leibnitz Beta Plateau, after the mountain's old informal name. In 2023 the IAU announced the name Mons Mouton, for NASA mathematician Melba Roy Mouton, and NASA's 2024 list uses it. NASA picked this area for its VIPER rover for drivable ground near shadowed areas. NASA ended VIPER in July 2024, then in 2025 chose Blue Origin to deliver it, aiming for late 2027.

verdicts.claim: IAU named the mountain Mons Mouton after Melba Roy Mouton on a VIPER-team proposal; formerly Leibnitz Beta; press release 16 Feb 2023 vs Wikipedia 13 May 2022.
verdicts.finalClaim: The IAU naming group approved the name Mons Mouton, honouring NASA mathematician Melba Roy Mouton, on a proposal from NASA's VIPER team; the mountain was sometimes called Leibnitz Beta. The IAU press release is dated 16 February 2023; the 13 May 2022 Gazetteer date was not confirmed.

verdicts.claim: NASA's 2022 list included 'Leibnitz Beta Plateau'; IAU says the mountain is one of 13 candidates; 'Mons Mouton' is on the 2024 list.
verdicts.finalClaim: NASA's 2022 list included Leibnitz Beta Plateau and the IAU release says the mountain is one of the 13 Artemis III candidate regions; NASA's 2024 list names Mons Mouton. verdicts.claim: Mons Mouton is flat-topped, nearly 100 km across, ~6,000 m above surroundings; LROC says it likely formed as part of the SPA rim.
verdicts.finalClaim: Mons Mouton is flat-topped, almost 100 km across and about 6,000 m above the surrounding terrain; LROC says it is thought to have formed as part of the South Pole-Aitken basin rim.

verdicts.claim: VIPER was to land at the western edge of Nobile on Mons Mouton (rover-accessible terrain, nearby PSRs); cancelled July 2024, revived Sept 2025; Blue Origin optional task order for late 2027.
verdicts.finalClaim: NASA chose the mountainous area west of Nobile crater (Mons Mouton) for VIPER for its rover-accessible terrain and nearby permanently shadowed areas. verdicts.finalClaim: IM-2 Athena landed on 6 March 2025 near the centre of Mons Mouton (LROC); its target is about 21 km north of (farther from the pole than) this region's 2022 centre (computed). Coordinate check: the catalog point is thus on the mountain's southern, pole-facing part.

verdicts.finalClaim: In October 2023 China named the area around Leibnitz Beta among four preliminary Chang'e-8 candidate landing areas.

verdicts.finalClaim: NASA says the hilltop is peppered with smaller rocks and pebbles and many craters.

sites.headline: Artemis III candidate region on Nobile crater's southwestern rim
sites.overview: Nobile Rim 1 is a NASA name for an Artemis III candidate landing region, not an IAU name. It lies on the southwestern rim of Nobile, a crater about 79 km across named after the Italian aviator and explorer Umberto Nobile. NASA listed it among 13 regions in August 2022, each about 15 by 15 km, and kept it among nine in October 2024. In 2021 NASA picked an area near Nobile's western edge for the VIPER rover. Intuitive Machines' Athena lander came down on its side at nearby Mons Mouton in March 2025. In 2026 NASA changed Artemis III to an Earth-orbit test flight.

verdicts.claim: officialName: 'Nobile Rim 1' is a NASA Artemis III candidate-region name, not an IAU name; Nobile crater is IAU-named after Umberto Nobile.
verdicts.finalClaim: Informal name: 'Nobile Rim 1' is a NASA Artemis III candidate-region name, not an IAU name. The crater Nobile is IAU-named after the Italian aviator and explorer Umberto Nobile.

verdicts.claim: setting: southwestern rim of Nobile (about 79 km across), Mons Mouton area on Nobile's western side, about 4.5 deg of latitude from the pole.
verdicts.finalClaim: On the southwestern rim of Nobile crater (about 79 km across), next to Mons Mouton, which shares its LROC mosaic. Catalog point -85.44, 37.44E is 4.56 deg of latitude from the pole. Geometry check (this run): the point is 39 km from Nobile's centre (85 deg 17'S, 53 deg 16'E per Wikipedia), about one crater radius, on the poleward-west side, so the catalog point agrees with 'southwestern rim'.

verdicts.claim: Nobile: IAU-named after Umberto Nobile; diameter 79.27 km; an older listing gives 73.54 km and the former name Scott A.
verdicts.finalClaim: Nobile is an impact crater near the south pole, named by the IAU in 1994 after the Italian aviator and explorer Umberto Nobile. Wikipedia gives 79.27 km across; the-moon.us gives 73.54 km. It was earlier labelled Scott A, a designation the USGS gazetteer lists as dropped and the-moon.us says was never IAU-approved.
verdicts.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobile_(crater) ; https://the-moon.us/wiki/Nobile ; https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Feature/13014 (WebSearch summaries; gazetteer page itself not opened)

verdicts.claim: NASA named Nobile Rim 1 among 13 regions on 19 Aug 2022; regions within six degrees of the pole, about 15 x 15 km; a landing site is about 100 m radius.
verdicts.finalClaim: NASA named Nobile Rim 1 among 13 Artemis III candidate landing regions in August 2022 (announced Friday 19 Aug). Each region is within six degrees of latitude of the south pole and about 15 by 15 km; a landing site is a spot of about 100 m radius within a region.

verdicts.claim: Kept in the list of nine announced 28 Oct 2024, no priority order; selection weighed science, launch windows, terrain, Earth communication, lighting.
verdicts.finalClaim: Nobile Rim 1 was kept in NASA's list of nine regions announced in October 2024 (at the LEAG meeting; reported 28 Oct), listed in no priority order. NASA weighed science potential, launch window availability, terrain suitability, communication with Earth and lighting.

verdicts.claim: In Sept 2021 NASA picked an area just west of Nobile (western edge, Mons Mouton) for VIPER, citing rover-accessible terrain and nearby PSRs; not known whether inside the Nobile Rim 1 region.
verdicts.finalClaim: On 20 Sept 2021 NASA picked a mountainous area near the western edge of Nobile crater as VIPER's landing site, citing rover-accessible terrain and nearby permanently shadowed areas. Sources read do not tie that site to the Nobile Rim 1 region or name it Mons Mouton.

verdicts.claim: VIPER was cancelled in 2024; in Sept 2025 NASA gave Blue Origin a CLPS task order to deliver VIPER in late 2027 on Blue Moon MK1; no landing site given.
verdicts.finalClaim: NASA announced on 17 July 2024 that it would cancel VIPER over cost growth and delays. On 19 Sept 2025 NASA gave Blue Origin CLPS task order CS-7: the base covers design work, and delivery of VIPER on a Blue Moon MK1 lander in late 2027 is an option NASA decides on later. No landing site is given.

verdicts.claim: IM-2 Athena touched down 6 March 2025 at about 84.79S, 29.20E at Mons Mouton, about 250 m from target, inside a crater, on its side; just north of the LROC NR1/Mons Mouton mosaic bounds.

That point is just north of the LROC Nobile Rim 1 / Mons Mouton mosaic (northern edge -84.82), so it is near this region, not shown to be inside it.

sites.headline: Artemis III candidate region on Nobile crater's northeastern rim
sites.overview: Nobile Rim 2 is a NASA name for an Artemis III candidate landing region, not an IAU name. It lies on the northeastern rim of Nobile crater, across the crater from Nobile Rim 1. NASA included it in the August 2022 list of 13 regions and kept it in the October 2024 list of nine. A 2024 study by Pena-Asensio and colleagues scored 1,247 possible landing points on visibility, sunlight, Earth contact, shadowed areas and geology; its nine best points all fell here. That ranking is the authors' own, not NASA's. In 2026 NASA changed Artemis III to an Earth-orbit test flight.

verdicts.claim: officialName: 'Nobile Rim 2' is a NASA candidate-region name, not IAU; Nobile is IAU-named after Umberto Nobile.
verdicts.finalClaim: Informal name: 'Nobile Rim 2' is a NASA Artemis III candidate-region name, not an IAU name. The crater Nobile is IAU-named after Umberto Nobile.

verdicts.claim: setting: northeastern rim of Nobile, opposite Nobile Rim 1, about 6 deg of latitude from the pole.
verdicts.finalClaim: On the northeastern rim of Nobile crater, across the crater from Nobile Rim 1, about 6 degrees of latitude from the pole. Geometry check (this run): the catalog point -83.95, 58.74E is 43 km from Nobile's centre (crater radius about 40 km), on the side away from the pole and to the east, so it agrees with 'northeastern rim'.

verdicts.claim: Region centre -83.95, 58.74E (Henriksen 2023 Table 1); LROC NAC_ROI_NOBILE02LO1 centred -83.9, 58.7E, bounds lat -84.40 to -83.50, lon 54.46 to 63.02E.

verdicts.finalClaim: Nobile crater is IAU-named (1994) after Umberto Nobile; Wikipedia gives 79.27 km across (the-moon.us gives 73.54 km).

verdicts.finalClaim: Nobile Rim 2 was one of NASA's 13 Artemis III candidate regions of August 2022 (each about 15 by 15 km, within six degrees of the pole) and was kept in the list of nine announced in October 2024.

sites.headline: Artemis III candidate region closest to the pole, at de Gerlache
sites.overview: de Gerlache Rim 2 is a NASA name for an Artemis III candidate landing region, not an IAU name. It lies at the rim of de Gerlache, a crater about 31 to 32 km across named after the Belgian Antarctic explorer Adrien de Gerlache. It was on NASA's 2022 list of 13 regions and is the closest to the south pole of the nine kept in October 2024. Its neighbour, de Gerlache Rim 1, was dropped. sites.headline: Where IM-1 Odysseus made the first commercial Moon landing, 2024
sites.overview: Intuitive Machines' IM-1 lander Odysseus landed here on 22 February 2024, the first commercial soft landing on the Moon and the first US soft landing since Apollo 17. The site is an intercrater area within about 1.5 km of its target near the crater Malapert A. NASA asked for this site to learn how to send data to Earth from a spot low on the lunar horizon. LRO images show the lander in a degraded crater about 1 km wide, on ground sloping about 12 degrees. Odysseus came in too fast and tipped, but NASA received data from all five active payloads.
